question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/470210fb9509e87c3e51a990bac7483e5862d2f37afdce9823279838e8391592.png)
question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/cc4019b4978cb96b931632ee2b6bf318b5eda46f4d9a73d252e76c7572285517.svg)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/458d9c56e8c1857546e7e112a9ad084fe7832781d448340ccfc141438a6eee78.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-1$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/d504ae47c4cfcd428a362d590d23713844d9ead5df792086a3bab07d41573bd8.svg)

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/9210f84189ff4a94c1a1dded19ff6e409c75be9d4e27f17d4d1a4d9ff44fcc0b.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/38e227b8bac9c4cb2ae93e2b29e1ca70576383a176dcf193350a9b464a4dd88f.svg)

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/7ef739bcc9a338d9535ab130a3bbe1cd46204bf7d8dbd55a49244abe9764a04a.svg)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{-t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/924dcd7002fa679bf3a0021099928c45fba82a5bf54ba157a21d846eb1587640.svg)
lie on the $y$-axis. Since $e^{-4t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/c5b1aa6ccde39c56b503e2d59a56e2ac8058b08495567f4e2cb40f6a056faedd.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t) = c_1e^{-t}$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{-4t}$ provided that $c_1,c_2 \neq 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-{c}_{1}{e}^{-t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14121715/assets/6c3af2fe68c4bcddbbfd9f13eb84e73014511374c0adc570084f9c92773d31e0.png)
